paragraphs.text: We have seen how death was already broken and inheritance already given. The remaining question is not doctrinal but practical: does that truth live in us, or merely sit in our minds as correct information?

Here is the plain instruction underneath everything else that will be said in this chapter: do not ever be afraid of death. That single line is not a slogan to be repeated comfortably; it is a command addressed to people who, if they are honest, still flinch at the subject.

Fear, when it shows up around death, is not something to be treated as a normal, expected human reaction that we simply manage. It is not normal. For the believer, going to heaven should be occasion for joy, not dread — so that when someone departs and enters heaven, the fitting response is gladness, not the heaviness that so often takes over a room.

Part of the reason this fear persists is that no one knows the set time. There is no fixed, revealed hour stamped on a life that would let a person calculate safety in advance. But the absence of a known hour is not meant to produce dread; it is meant to be held alongside the assurance that whenever the hour comes, it is gain, not loss.

It needs to be said plainly: fearing death is an abuse. It is an abuse to your own person, a mistreatment of the very life and identity that belongs to you in Christ. And it is not new. The devil has used this particular strategy for a very long time, and he has not changed his style. The weapon is old, recycled, worn smooth from long use — and it still works on people who have never been told to resist it.
Naming the strategy is one thing. Recognizing it operating even among the convinced is another, and sobering.

Of recent, there have been reports of the deaths of a number of supposed children of God who did not embrace death as gain. Whenever word comes that a child of God has gone and given account to God, the first question worth asking is simple: how were the last hours? And too often the answer that comes back is troubling — he died saying, I don't want to die now, or she died saying the same. That pattern is sincerely worrying, because it raises the question of whether the church has actually been filled enough with this truth, or has only been told about it.

This is exactly why death as gain cannot remain an idea admired from a safe intellectual distance. It is not mind over matter — it is not a technique of positive thinking applied at the last moment to overpower natural terror. It must be your reality. Not a doctrine filed away for later, not a verse quoted at funerals, but the actual ground a person is standing on when the hour comes.

This is where Paul's own confession becomes the test case. The question under discussion was Philippians chapter one, verse twenty-one — to live is Christ, and to die is gain. Paul could say that anything he might go on living would still be Christ; life itself, in all its ordinary continuation, was nothing other than Christ being lived out. Christ is my life, Paul says, in effect. To live is Christ.

But that confession was not abstract theology for Paul, and it cannot be abstract theology for anyone who repeats it. If you don't practice Christ, death will be difficult for you. You have got to practice Christ — not merely believe a statement about him, not merely know the verse, but actually live out his life as your own day by day. If you are not practicing life now, death will be heavy when it comes. The weight a person carries at the end is, in large part, the weight of what was or was not practiced beforehand.
Set against that warning, there is also a demonstration — proof that the thing being described is not theory.

At least two men are known whose departures bore this out. Each knew, in advance, the exact hour and the exact date of his own death. There was no panic in that knowledge, no scramble to rearrange affairs out of terror. Instead there was a settled readiness that allowed each man to say to those around him, in effect, so you had better come — and then, without struggle, I'll go to heaven. That is what it looks like when death as gain has stopped being a sentence recited and become the reality a person is actually living out of.

The contrast could not be sharper: on one side, believers startled at the threshold, still asking not to die; on the other, believers who named the hour and walked into it in peace. The difference was not the amount of doctrine known, but the amount of Christ practiced.
